definition: Capability lost as a side effect of safety and alignment training (over-refusal, hedging, reduced creativity).
details: Capability lost as a side effect of safety and alignment training (over-refusal, hedging, reduced creativity). Modern post-training aims to minimize it; measuring it requires capability benchmarks alongside safety benchmarks.

explainer.lead: Alignment tax is the usefulness a model loses while being trained to behave more safely, such as refusing harmless requests, hedging excessively, or becoming less creative. It matters because a better safety score can hide a model that has become noticeably less capable.

tiers.eli5: Imagine teaching a helpful robot to be careful, but it becomes so cautious that it refuses to help build a paper airplane. The lost helpfulness is the alignment tax. The goal is to keep the robot safe without making it needlessly less useful.
tiers.practitioner: Compare capability benchmarks before and after alignment post-training, and read the results alongside safety benchmarks. Watch for over-refusal, excessive hedging, and reduced creativity when assessing the trade-off. A common pitfall is treating improved safety scores alone as evidence of a better model.
tiers.paperLevel: For a capability benchmark B, a simple comparison is tax(B) = S_base(B) - S_aligned(B), where a positive value indicates capability lost after alignment training. This quantity is benchmark-dependent and does not by itself capture every form of over-refusal, hedging, or creativity loss. It should therefore be interpreted alongside changes in safety-benchmark results.

explainer.example: A starting model solves 80 of 100 coding tasks, but its aligned version solves 72 and refuses more harmless requests. The 8-task drop on that benchmark is an alignment tax; separate safety results show what the trade-off gained.

usedIn.name: LLM post-training
usedIn.detail: Compare models before and after alignment training to identify capability lost while improving safety.

usedIn.name: Safety evaluation
usedIn.detail: Interpret safety-benchmark results together with capability results so improvements do not conceal regressions.

usedIn.name: Model development
usedIn.detail: Use the trade-off to guide post-training that limits over-refusal, hedging, and reduced creativity.

explainer.intuition: Safety training can push a model away from unwanted behavior, but the same pressure can also suppress useful behavior. Alignment tax names that collateral loss rather than the safety benefit itself.
howItWorks: Measure the aligned model on the same capability benchmarks.
Treat capability losses as the tax and weigh them against safety gains.
explainer.whyItMatters: It makes hidden costs of alignment visible and gives post-training a concrete target: retain capability while improving safety. Measuring both sides prevents safety gains from being mistaken for overall improvement.
misconceptions: It is not a financial charge or a deliberate performance limit.
Not every behavior changed by safety training counts as lost capability.
A better safety score alone does not show whether the tax is small or large.

diagram.caption: Alignment tax is estimated from capability changes, while safety benchmarks show the other side of the trade-off.
